CHAPTER 1.1 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.1 · LEARNING AREA 1 · AUGUST · SEPTEMBER

Representing fractions

Half a pizza, 0.5 litres of juice, 50% off: that is the same number three times, just written differently. In this chapter you learn to convert confidently between the three ways of writing it: fraction, decimal and percentage. You find out why some decimals never stop, and you sort numbers into sets.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • write a fractional number as a fraction, as a decimal and as a percentage
  • convert without long division
  • tell terminating and recurring decimals apart
  • compare fractional numbers and put them in order on the number line
  • work with the words set, element and subset
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

How many minutes are a quarter of an hour?

$\tfrac14$ of 60 minutes is 15 minutes.

Expand $\tfrac35$ to the denominator 10. Which numerator is on top?

$\tfrac35 = \tfrac{3 \cdot 2}{5 \cdot 2} = \tfrac{6}{10}$

Simplify $\tfrac{12}{16}$ as far as possible. Which denominator is left?

$\tfrac{12}{16} = \tfrac{12 : 4}{16 : 4} = \tfrac34$

Which number lies exactly halfway between 0 and 1? Write it as a fraction.

$\tfrac12$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Fraction, decimal, percentage

Each pizza is cut into four quarters. That makes twelve quarters for four people, so three quarters for each: $\tfrac34$ of a pizza. You can also calculate: $3 : 4 = \tfrac34$. A fraction is a division that has not been worked out yet.

In the fraction $\tfrac34$ the denominator 4 says into how many equal parts the whole is divided. The numerator 3 says how many parts you take.

A decimal writes tenths, hundredths and thousandths after the decimal point: $0.75$ means 7 tenths and 5 hundredths, so $\tfrac{75}{100}$. That is why you can often convert without dividing: you expand the fraction to the denominator 10, 100 or 1000.

Per cent means “out of a hundred”. $75\%$ is just another name for $\tfrac{75}{100}$.

KEY POINT · THREE WAYS OF WRITING

$\tfrac34 = \tfrac{75}{100} = 0.75 = 75\%$   (expanded by 25)

Fraction → decimal: expand to 10, 100, 1000 …, then write the numerator after the decimal point.

Decimal → fraction: count the decimal places. $0.125 = \tfrac{125}{1000} = \tfrac18$. Then simplify.

Percentage: $p\% = \tfrac{p}{100}$. From a decimal to a percentage: move the decimal point two places to the right.

Learn by heart: $\tfrac12 = 0.5 = 50\%$ · $\tfrac14 = 0.25$ · $\tfrac34 = 0.75$ · $\tfrac15 = 0.2$ · $\tfrac18 = 0.125$ · $\tfrac1{10} = 0.1$

Careful: $0.5$ is not $\tfrac15$. One place after the decimal point means tenths: $0.5 = \tfrac{5}{10}$.

INTERACTIVE · ONE FRACTION, THREE WAYS OF WRITING

Set the numerator and the denominator. On the right you see the same number as a decimal and as a percentage.

EXAMPLE 1 · FROM FRACTION TO DECIMAL

Write $\tfrac{7}{20}$ as a decimal and as a percentage.

20 times 5 is 100. So expand by 5: $\tfrac{7}{20} = \tfrac{35}{100}$.

$\tfrac{7}{20} = 0.35 = 35\%$

EXAMPLE 2 · FROM DECIMAL TO FRACTION

Write $0.64$ as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Two decimal places: hundredths. $0.64 = \tfrac{64}{100}$. Divide both numbers by 4.

$0.64 = \tfrac{16}{25}$

EXERCISES

Write as a decimal and as a percentage: a) $\tfrac{3}{10}$   b) $\tfrac{2}{5}$   c) $\tfrac{9}{25}$   d) $\tfrac{1}{4}$   e) $\tfrac{11}{50}$

Expand so that the bottom is 10 or 100.

a) $0.3 = 30\%$   b) $0.4 = 40\%$   c) $0.36 = 36\%$   d) $0.25 = 25\%$   e) $0.22 = 22\%$

Write as a fraction in its lowest terms: a) $0.7$   b) $0.25$   c) $0.08$   d) $0.375$   e) $1.5$

a) $\tfrac{7}{10}$   b) $\tfrac14$   c) $\tfrac{8}{100} = \tfrac{2}{25}$   d) $\tfrac{375}{1000} = \tfrac38$   e) $\tfrac{15}{10} = \tfrac32$

There are 25 pupils in a class. 8 of them cycle to school. What fraction is that, as a fraction, as a decimal and as a percentage?

$\tfrac{8}{25} = \tfrac{32}{100} = 0.32 = 32\%$

Which number is the odd one out? $\tfrac{3}{5}$   $0.6$   $60\%$   $\tfrac{6}{10}$   $0.06$   $\tfrac{12}{20}$

$0.06 = 6\%$. All the others are $0.6$.

A fraction has the denominator 40 and is equal to $0.375$. What is it? Can you find a second fraction with the denominator 8 that lies between $0.375$ and $0.5$?

$0.375 = \tfrac38$. Expand to 40.

$\tfrac38 = \tfrac{15}{40}$. Between $\tfrac38$ and $\tfrac48 = 0.5$ there is no fraction with the denominator 8. With the denominator 16 it works: $\tfrac{7}{16} = 0.4375$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Write $\tfrac{9}{20}$ as a decimal.

$\tfrac{9}{20} = \tfrac{45}{100} = 0.45$

What percentage is $\tfrac45$?

$\tfrac45 = \tfrac{80}{100} = 80\%$

Write $0.125$ as a fraction in its lowest terms.

$\tfrac{125}{1000} = \tfrac18$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Terminating or recurring

For $1 : 3$ the calculator shows $0.3333333$. If you carry on by hand, the remainder is always 1. That is why a 3 comes again and again. The decimal never stops. On the other hand, $1 : 8 = 0.125$ is finished after three places.

A decimal in which a sequence of digits repeats for ever is called recurring. The repeating sequence is called the period. You write it only once and put a bar over it: $0.333\ldots = 0.\overline{3}$ and $0.1666\ldots = 0.1\overline{6}$.

Whether a fraction terminates or recurs can be seen from the simplified denominator. Only if it can be expanded to 10, 100, 1000 … does the decimal stop. That works exactly when the denominator has only the factors 2 and 5. Because $10 = 2 \cdot 5$.

KEY POINT · TERMINATING OR RECURRING

Simplify the fraction completely and split the denominator into factors.

Only 2 and 5 in the denominator: the decimal terminates.   $\tfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$, because $8 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2$.

Another factor in the denominator (3, 7, 11 …): the decimal recurs.   $\tfrac{5}{6} = 0.8\overline{3}$, because $6 = 2 \cdot 3$.

Simplify first: $\tfrac{3}{12}$ has the denominator 12 with the factor 3. But simplified it is $\tfrac14 = 0.25$, so it terminates.

The calculator rounds the last place: $2 : 3$ often shows $0.6666667$. Correct is $0.\overline{6}$.

INTERACTIVE · DOES IT STOP?

Try the denominators 1 to 12. Which give terminating decimals? The reason is shown on the right.

EXAMPLE 3 · PREDICTING

Decide without calculating: is $\tfrac{7}{40}$ terminating or recurring? And $\tfrac{7}{30}$?

$40 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 5$: only 2 and 5, so it terminates. $\tfrac{7}{40} = \tfrac{175}{1000} = 0.175$.

$30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ contains the 3: recurring, $\tfrac{7}{30} = 0.2\overline{3}$

EXAMPLE 4 · ORDERING

Put in order of size: $\tfrac23$, $0.6$, $\tfrac58$, $0.66$.

All as decimals: $\tfrac23 = 0.666\ldots$, $0.6$, $\tfrac58 = 0.625$, $0.66$. Compare place by place.

$0.6 < \tfrac58 < 0.66 < \tfrac23$

EXERCISES

Write with a recurring bar: a) $0.777\ldots$   b) $0.121212\ldots$   c) $2.4555\ldots$   d) $0.142857142857\ldots$

a) $0.\overline{7}$   b) $0.\overline{12}$   c) $2.4\overline{5}$   d) $0.\overline{142857}$

Terminating or recurring? Decide from the denominator: a) $\tfrac{1}{16}$   b) $\tfrac{2}{9}$   c) $\tfrac{3}{25}$   d) $\tfrac{5}{12}$   e) $\tfrac{9}{15}$

For e) simplify first.

a) terminating, $0.0625$   b) recurring, $0.\overline{2}$   c) terminating, $0.12$   d) recurring, $0.41\overline{6}$   e) $\tfrac{9}{15} = \tfrac35 = 0.6$, terminating

Calculate $\tfrac19$, $\tfrac29$ and $\tfrac39$ with the calculator. Predict $\tfrac59$ and $\tfrac89$. What does $\tfrac99$ give then?

$\tfrac19 = 0.\overline{1}$, $\tfrac29 = 0.\overline{2}$, $\tfrac39 = 0.\overline{3}$. So $\tfrac59 = 0.\overline{5}$ and $\tfrac89 = 0.\overline{8}$. Following the pattern, $\tfrac99$ would be $0.\overline{9}$. But $\tfrac99 = 1$. In fact $0.\overline{9}$ is exactly 1, just written differently.

Put in order from smallest to largest: $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $0.7$, $\tfrac{7}{9}$, $0.75$, $\tfrac{4}{5}$.

$0.7 < \tfrac34 = 0.75 < \tfrac79 = 0.\overline{7} < \tfrac45 = 0.8$. The numbers $\tfrac34$ and $0.75$ are equal.

Find all denominators from 2 to 30 for which $\tfrac{1}{n}$ is a terminating decimal.

The denominator may only consist of twos and fives.

2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 16, 20, 25. That is eight denominators.

TEST YOURSELF!

Write $\tfrac{7}{40}$ as a decimal.

$\tfrac{7}{40} = \tfrac{175}{1000} = 0.175$

$\tfrac{1}{3} = 0.\overline{x}$. Which digit is $x$?

$0.\overline{3}$

How many of the fractions $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac14$, $\tfrac15$, $\tfrac16$, $\tfrac17$, $\tfrac18$, $\tfrac{1}{10}$ give terminating decimals?

$\tfrac12$, $\tfrac14$, $\tfrac15$, $\tfrac18$, $\tfrac{1}{10}$: five of them.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Number ranges and sets

With the natural numbers $0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ you can count. But $3 : 4$ does not work out there. You need new numbers: fractions. With them every division works, except division by zero. The range of numbers becomes larger.

In mathematics you collect things into a set and write them in curly brackets: $T = \{1, 2, 3, 6\}$ is the set of the factors of 6. The things in the set are called elements. You write $2 \in T$ (“2 is an element of $T$”) and $5 \notin T$ (“5 is not an element of $T$”).

If one set lies completely inside another, it is called a subset: $\{1, 2\} \subset T$. In a Venn diagram sets are drawn as areas; a subset lies inside.

The fractional numbers are all numbers that can be written as a fraction. Their set is called $\mathbb{Q}^+$. Every natural number belongs to it, because $5 = \tfrac51$.

KEY POINT · SETS AND NUMBER RANGES

$\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$: the natural numbers   ·   $\mathbb{Q}^+$: the fractional numbers

$\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Q}^+$: every natural number is also a fractional number, but not the other way round: $\tfrac12 \in \mathbb{Q}^+$, $\tfrac12 \notin \mathbb{N}$.

In $\mathbb{Q}^+$ you can carry out every division, except by 0. Between two fractional numbers there is always another one.

Zero: at school it counts as a natural number. Some books start at 1.

Equal, but written differently: $\tfrac{12}{4}$, $3.0$ and $300\%$ are all the natural number 3.

INTERACTIVE · WHERE DOES THE NUMBER BELONG?

Decide for each number: is it a natural number, or only a fractional one? It then lands in the diagram.

EXAMPLE 5 · SETS OF FACTORS

$T_{12}$ is the set of the factors of 12, $T_{6}$ the set of the factors of 6. Write both down. Is $T_6 \subset T_{12}$?

$T_{12} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12\}$, $T_6 = \{1, 2, 3, 6\}$. Every element of $T_6$ is also in $T_{12}$.

Yes, $T_6 \subset T_{12}$. But $4 \in T_{12}$ and $4 \notin T_6$.

EXAMPLE 6 · ALWAYS ANOTHER ONE IN BETWEEN

Find a fractional number between $\tfrac13$ and $\tfrac12$.

Give them a common denominator: $\tfrac13 = \tfrac{4}{12}$, $\tfrac12 = \tfrac{6}{12}$. In between lies $\tfrac{5}{12}$.

$\tfrac13 < \tfrac{5}{12} < \tfrac12$. Between two natural numbers such as 3 and 4, on the other hand, there is no natural number.

EXERCISES

Fill in $\in$ or $\notin$: a) $7 \;\square\; \mathbb{N}$   b) $\tfrac23 \;\square\; \mathbb{N}$   c) $\tfrac23 \;\square\; \mathbb{Q}^+$   d) $\tfrac{20}{5} \;\square\; \mathbb{N}$   e) $0.1 \;\square\; \mathbb{Q}^+$

a) $\in$   b) $\notin$   c) $\in$   d) $\in$, because $\tfrac{20}{5} = 4$   e) $\in$

Write the set in brackets: a) the factors of 18   b) the multiples of 4 that are less than 30   c) the even numbers between 9 and 19

a) $\{1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18\}$   b) $\{0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28\}$   c) $\{10, 12, 14, 16, 18\}$

$A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12\}$ and $B = \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$. Draw a Venn diagram with two overlapping areas. Which numbers lie in both?

In both: 1, 2 and 4. Only in $A$: 3, 6, 12. Only in $B$: 8. $B$ is not a subset of $A$, because $8 \notin A$.

Find three fractional numbers between $0.2$ and $0.3$. Then find one between $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{2}{7}$.

For example $0.21$, $0.25$, $0.29$. Between $\tfrac14 = \tfrac{7}{28}$ and $\tfrac27 = \tfrac{8}{28}$: expand to $\tfrac{14}{56}$ and $\tfrac{16}{56}$; in between lies $\tfrac{15}{56}$.

Lea says: “Between $\tfrac13$ and $\tfrac12$ there are exactly five fractions with the denominator 24.” Is that right? How many are there with the denominator 48?

$\tfrac13 = \tfrac{8}{24}$ and $\tfrac12 = \tfrac{12}{24}$.

No: between $\tfrac{8}{24}$ and $\tfrac{12}{24}$ there are only $\tfrac{9}{24}$, $\tfrac{10}{24}$, $\tfrac{11}{24}$, so three. With the denominator 48: from $\tfrac{17}{48}$ to $\tfrac{23}{48}$, so seven. With larger denominators there are more and more.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many elements does the set of the factors of 12 have?

$\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12\}$: six elements.

Which natural number is $\tfrac{28}{7}$?

$28 : 7 = 4$

Which fraction lies exactly halfway between $\tfrac13$ and $\tfrac12$?

$\tfrac{4}{12}$ and $\tfrac{6}{12}$: halfway between lies $\tfrac{5}{12}$.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Connecting with quantities: write as a number with the unit: a) $\tfrac34$ kg in grams   b) $\tfrac14$ h in minutes   c) $\tfrac{3}{5}$ m in centimetres   d) $0.2$ ℓ in millilitres

a) 750 g   b) 15 min   c) 60 cm   d) 200 mℓ

One sports shop gives “a quarter off” football boots, another “$20\%$ off”. Where do you save more?

A quarter is $25\%$. The first shop gives more off.

Max took 20 penalties and scored 17; Ina took 25 and scored 21. Who is the better penalty taker? Calculate in per cent.

Max: $\tfrac{17}{20} = \tfrac{85}{100} = 85\%$. Ina: $\tfrac{21}{25} = \tfrac{84}{100} = 84\%$. Max scores slightly more often.

Write $0.\overline{3}$ and $0.\overline{6}$ as fractions. What could $0.\overline{27}$ be as a fraction? Check with the calculator.

$\tfrac19 = 0.\overline{1}$ and $\tfrac{1}{99} = 0.\overline{01}$.

$0.\overline{3} = \tfrac13$, $0.\overline{6} = \tfrac23$. Because $\tfrac{1}{99} = 0.\overline{01}$, $0.\overline{27} = \tfrac{27}{99} = \tfrac{3}{11}$. Check: $3 : 11 = 0.2727\ldots$

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Fractions in ancient Egypt

One of the oldest mathematical writings in the world is a papyrus roll from Egypt, written around 1550 BC by a scribe called Ahmes. Today it is named after a later buyer, the Rhind Papyrus, and it is in the British Museum in London.

The Egyptians wrote fractions almost only as unit fractions, that is with the numerator 1: $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac14$ and so on. Only for $\tfrac23$ did they have a sign of its own. If they wanted to write $\tfrac25$, they split the number into different unit fractions: $\tfrac25 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{1}{15}$. At the beginning of the papyrus there is a long table that gives such splittings for $\tfrac25$, $\tfrac27$, $\tfrac29$ up to $\tfrac{2}{101}$.

Try it yourself: check $\tfrac25 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{1}{15}$ by giving the fractions a common denominator. Can you find a way of splitting $\tfrac34$ into two different unit fractions?

$\tfrac13 + \tfrac{1}{15} = \tfrac{5}{15} + \tfrac{1}{15} = \tfrac{6}{15} = \tfrac25$. And $\tfrac34 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac14$.

Source: Rhind Papyrus, Thebes, around 1550 BC, scribe Ahmes; British Museum, London (BM 10057 and 10058). The “2/n table” is at the beginning of the roll.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

THREE WAYS OF WRITING

Fraction, decimal, percentage: expand to 10, 100, 1000

$\tfrac{7}{20} = \tfrac{35}{100} = 0.35 = 35\%$

BACK TO THE FRACTION

Count the decimal places, then simplify

$0.125 = \tfrac{125}{1000} = \tfrac18$

TERMINATING OR RECURRING

Simplified denominator made only of 2 and 5: terminating, otherwise recurring

$\tfrac38 = 0.375$ · $\tfrac56 = 0.8\overline{3}$

SETS

Element $\in$, not an element $\notin$, subset $\subset$

$\{1, 2\} \subset \{1, 2, 3, 6\}$

NUMBER RANGES

$\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Q}^+$: every natural number is also a fractional number

$\tfrac{12}{4} = 3 \in \mathbb{N}$, $\tfrac34 \notin \mathbb{N}$

TESTTWO ROUNDS · INSTANT FEEDBACK
ROUND 1 · WITHOUT A CALCULATOR

Write $\tfrac35$ as a decimal.

$\tfrac35 = \tfrac{6}{10} = 0.6$

What percentage is $0.12$?

$0.12 = \tfrac{12}{100} = 12\%$

Write $15\%$ as a fraction in its lowest terms.

$\tfrac{15}{100} = \tfrac{3}{20}$

ROUND 2 · THINKING

$\tfrac{5}{6} = 0.8\overline{x}$. Which digit is $x$?

$5 : 6 = 0.8333\ldots = 0.8\overline{3}$

Write $\tfrac{15}{40}$ as a decimal.

$\tfrac{15}{40} = \tfrac38 = 0.375$

$M$ is the set of all natural numbers that are greater than 2 and less than 7. How many elements does $M$ have?

$\{3, 4, 5, 6\}$: four elements.
